title: Route.put() Requires a Callback Function but Got [object Undefined] — What It Means and How to Fix It
subtitle: A deep-dive into one of Express.js's most common and confusing startup crashes — why it happens, what Node is actually telling you, and how to never see it again.
content:
Route.put() Requires a Callback Function but Got [object Undefined]

You just wrote some new routes. You save the file, nodemon restarts, and then — boom. The server crashes before it even starts listening. The terminal throws this at you:

Error: Route.put() requires a callback function but got a [object Undefined]
    at Route.<computed> [as put] (express/lib/router/route.js:216:15)
    at file:///your-project/routes/marketRoutes.js:27:8

Your first reaction is probably confusion. You did pass a function. You can see it right there in the route file. So what is Express complaining about?

Take a breath. This error is actually one of the most helpful crashes Express can throw at you — once you understand what it is really saying.

What Express Is Actually Telling You

Let's read the error message carefully. It says: "requires a callback function but got [object Undefined]".

That last part is the key. [object Undefined] means the value you passed as the route handler is undefined. Not a wrong function. Not a broken function. Literally nothing. An empty slot.

Express received something like this:

router.put('/products/:id/like', protect, undefined);

Of course Express panics. You told it "when someone hits this route, run this handler" — but the handler doesn't exist.

The Real Culprit: A Missing or Misnamed Export

Here is the thing. You almost certainly did not type undefined yourself. What actually happened is that you imported a function that does not exist under that name.

Look at this line from a real route file:

import * as productController from '../controllers/marketProductController.js';

router.put('/products/:id/like', protect, productController.likeProduct);

This looks perfectly fine. But what if likeProduct was never exported from marketProductController.js? Or what if it was exported with a slightly different name — like toggleLike or likeProductHandler?

When you use import * as productController, you get an object containing every named export from that file. If likeProduct is not in that object, then productController.likeProduct evaluates to undefined. And that undefined gets passed straight into router.put().

Express sees it. Express throws. Server dies.

Why Does It Crash at Startup and Not at Request Time?

This is a question a lot of developers ask. Why doesn't Express just wait until someone actually hits that route to complain?

Because Express validates your route registrations immediately when the route file is loaded — not lazily when a request arrives. The moment Node.js imports your routes file, Express runs through every router.get(), router.post(), router.put() call and checks that each argument is actually a function.

Think of it like a restaurant kitchen. When the chef sets up the station before service, they check that every tool is in place. They do not wait for a customer to order a steak and then discover the knife is missing. Express does the same thing — it validates the setup before opening the doors.

This is actually a good thing. It means you catch the problem immediately at startup instead of discovering it at 2am when a real user hits that route in production.

How to Find and Fix It

The error message gives you the exact file and line number. In this case:

at file:///C:/Codalina/codalina-backend/routes/marketRoutes.js:27:8

Go to line 27 of marketRoutes.js. You will see something like:

router.put('/products/:id/like', protect, productController.likeProduct);

Now open the controller file it is importing from. Search for the export. Ask yourself three questions:

  1. Is the function actually defined in this file?
  2. Is it exported with export const or export function?
  3. Is the name spelled exactly the same in both files?

In the real example that caused this crash, the controller file did have likeProduct defined and exported correctly. So the fix was simply making sure the import and the usage matched perfectly. One typo, one missing export — that is all it takes.

⚠️ Quick Checklist: If you see this error, check these four things in order — (1) Is the function exported from the controller? (2) Is the import path correct? (3) Is the function name spelled identically in both files? (4) Did you accidentally export a default instead of a named export?

Default Export vs Named Export — A Common Trap

There is another version of this bug that catches people off guard. It happens when you mix up default and named exports.

Say your controller file does this:

// controller.js
const likeProduct = async (req, res) => { ... };

export default likeProduct; // Default export

But your route file does this:

// routes.js
import * as productController from './controller.js';

router.put('/like', productController.likeProduct); // undefined!

When you use import * as productController, you get an object of all named exports. A default export does not appear as a named property. So productController.likeProduct is undefined again.

The fix is to either switch to a named export in the controller, or change the import style in the routes file to match what the controller actually exports. Consistency is everything here.

The Broader Lesson: JavaScript Fails Silently on Missing Properties

Here is the deeper thing to understand. JavaScript does not throw an error when you access a property that does not exist on an object. It just quietly returns undefined.

const obj = { name: 'Imran' };
console.log(obj.age); // undefined — no error, no warning

This is by design. JavaScript is flexible. But that flexibility means bugs like this can slip through without any warning — right up until the moment you pass that undefined somewhere that actually checks it, like Express does.

Express is doing you a favor by being strict here. Many other parts of your codebase will not be. So when you see [object Undefined] in an error message, your first instinct should always be: something I imported does not exist under the name I used.

One More Thing: The Stack Trace Is Your Friend

A lot of developers see a wall of red text in the terminal and immediately feel overwhelmed. But the stack trace is not your enemy — it is a map.

Read it from top to bottom. The first line tells you the error type and message. The lines below it show you the call chain — which file called which function, in what order, leading up to the crash. The line that mentions your file (not a node_modules path) is almost always where the problem lives.

Error: Route.put() requires a callback function but got a [object Undefined]
    at Route.<computed> [as put] (node_modules/express/lib/router/route.js:216)
    at file:///C:/Codalina/codalina-backend/routes/marketRoutes.js:27:8  <-- THIS ONE

Line 27, column 8. That is your starting point. Everything else is Express's internal code doing its job. You only need to care about the line that points to your project.

Summary

This error means one thing: you passed undefined as a route handler to Express. It almost always happens because a function was not exported from the controller, was exported under a different name, or the import path was wrong. Express catches it at startup — which is actually helpful. Read the stack trace, find your file in it, check the export and import names match exactly, and the fix is usually a one-line correction. The error looks scary. The cause is almost always simple.
